summary: Defines how to use the Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS) compression algorithm inside the TLS protocol. TLS lets two sides negotiate lossless compression, but its only standard method at the time was no compression at all.

eli5.summary: Before sending a suitcase through a secure tunnel, you squeeze the clothes down so they take less room. This memo describes one way to squeeze them.

questions: how to compress data in tls
what is the tls compression method number for lzs
subtitle: How to squeeze TLS record payloads with the LZS algorithm, using compression method number 64.

tldr.problem: TLS can negotiate a compression method, but its only standard one was null, which means no compression. That left no interoperable way to save bandwidth on long-lived or high-volume TLS connections such as VPNs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an LZS compression method for TLS. Each record gets a one-byte header with a reset bit and a compressed/uncompressed bit, and the compressor keeps a 2,048-byte history across the records of one session.
tldr.outcome: LZS gets compression method identifier 64 from IANA. The RFC warns that compressing before encrypting can leak information through message length, and that the history holds plaintext. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3943 is an Informational document and it is updated by RFC 8996. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why TLS Needed a Compression Method
sections.content:
The TLS Handshake Protocol lets two sides negotiate a lossless compression method, and the TLS Record Protocol then applies it. TLS itself defined only CompressionMethod.null, which means no compression. The RFC says this kept implementations interoperable but made it hard to build interoperable ones that compress.

The author points to long-lived connections that move thousands or millions of octets, such as TLS used as an alternative VPN connection. Compression has long been associated with IPSec and PPTP VPNs, so adding it to TLS VPNs preserves that user experience. This document adds one method, based on the Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS) algorithm, and assumes you already know RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0).
sections.eli5: The only choice in TLS was to send everything at full size. Big downloads over a secure tunnel would be faster if the bags were squeezed first, so this memo adds a way to do that.

sections.title: The LZS Compression Method
sections.content:
The LZS CompressionMethod is a 16-bit index, negotiated as described in RFC 2246 and RFC 3749. IANA assigned 64 (0x40) as the identifier, from the Specification Required pool of the registry that RFC 3749 describes.

LZS here is stateful: the compressor keeps its history across all the records of a session. The RFC says there is little known benefit in a stateless method inside TLS. LZS uses a sliding window of 2,048 bytes, replaces repeated sequences with short tokens and recovers the original data exactly. It can compress strings as short as two octets.
sections.eli5: Both sides agree on a secret code word, number 64, that means we squeeze our bags with LZS. They also both remember the last bit of what they sent, which helps squeeze the next bag even smaller.

sections.title: The One-Byte TLSComp Header
sections.content:
After compression, the record payload (TLSCompressed.fragment) is an 8-bit TLSComp header followed by the data, which is either compressed or left uncompressed. The header is a single Flags octet.

  • Res: six reserved bits. They MUST be zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver.
  • RST: tells the peer that the compression history was reset before this record was compressed. It MUST be 1 on the first compressed record of a session.
  • C/U: 1 means the data is compressed, 0 means it is uncompressed.

The compressed data uses the encoding in ANSI X3.241, which the RFC shows for information only and which is also described in RFC 1967, RFC 1974 and RFC 2395. A compressed payload ends with an end marker, and the payload size MUST be a whole number of octets.
sections.eli5: Every package gets a tiny sticker. One part of the sticker says start remembering from scratch, and another says whether this package was squeezed or not.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Records
sections.content:
The sender MUST reset the compression history before compressing the first record after the TLS handshake completes. It MUST keep a separate history for each open TLS session, and it MUST "flush" the compressor on every compressed record. Flushing means all input is included in the output, so a record's data never spills into a later record. That matters because the compressed data must stay in step with the authenticated and encrypted TLS record.

The receiver MUST reset its decompression history before the first compressed record. After a record is received and decrypted, it MUST check the RST and C/U bits. If C/U is 1, it decompresses the data. If C/U is 0, it adds the uncompressed data to its history. If RST is 1, the receiver MAY reset its history first, although the RFC notes a reset is not required for the Hifn LZS algorithm.
sections.eli5: Each side keeps a notebook of recent messages for the one connection. At the end of every message the sender empties its hands so nothing is left over for the next one, and the receiver checks the sticker to know what to do.

sections.title: When Compression Makes Data Bigger
sections.content:
Any compressor can occasionally expand its input. The worst-case expansion for LZS is 12.5%, so TLS records of 15K bytes can never exceed the expansion limits of section 6.2.2 of RFC 2246. If a 16K-byte record expands past 17K bytes, the uncompressed version MUST be sent with the C/U bit set to 0.

For records that expand, the RFC lists three options. Sending the expanded data and keeping the history is workable. Sending the original data and keeping the history is the preferred option and SHOULD be implemented, because the receiver updates its own history from the uncompressed data. Sending the original data and clearing the history SHOULD NOT be implemented, since it may lose future compression.
sections.eli5: Sometimes squeezing a bag makes it bigger. Then you just send the bag as it was, but you both still write down what was in it so the next bag can be squeezed well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not change the TLS threat model, but compression combined with encryption can reveal information. The same data can compress to different lengths, so an observer who sees the length of the compressed data may learn about the original. Some ciphersuites do not hide length at all, such as stream ciphers without padding, and CBC with padding hides it only to some extent. Use of TLS compression SHOULD take this into account.

The LZS history holds the last 2K bytes of plaintext. Implementations MUST use separate histories for each TLS session, because a shared history could leak data between sessions. When a session ends they SHOULD treat the history like any plaintext, for example by freeing the memory and overwriting its contents, as they would TLS key material.
sections.eli5: If someone can see how big your package is, they might guess what is inside it. And the notebook of recent messages should be shredded when you are done with it.

fields.name: Res
fields.desc: Reserved. MUST be zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: RST
fields.desc: 1 means the compression history was reset before this record.

fields.name: C/U
fields.desc: 1 means compressed data, 0 means uncompressed data.
